summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children & Youth Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment for the caseworker, the court held that forcing a father from his home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the family's substantive due process rights because the caseworker lacked objectively reasonable grounds to suspect abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Protective action requires reasonable and articulable evidence of abuse or imminent danger.
key_cases.quote: we hold that she lacked objectively reasonable grounds to believe the child had been sexually abused or was in imminent danger of sexual abuse

key_cases.case_name: Good v. Dauphin County Social Services for Children & Youth
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment on qualified immunity, holding that on the mother's version of the facts a caseworker and police officer entered the home and strip-searched the child without valid consent, a warrant, or exigent circumstances, violating clearly established law.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the emergency exception: imminent danger of serious bodily injury with intrusion reasonably necessary to avert it.
key_cases.quote: under these circumstances a reasonable law enforcement officer could not have believed Ms. Good had given legally effective consent to either the entry or the subsequent strip search

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers' ex parte presentations to the judge that stripped the mother of custody violated procedural due process, but that the individual caseworkers were absolutely immune, and remanded for trial on the county's liability.
key_cases.relevance: Distinguishes genuine emergencies, where ex parte action may be tolerated, from non-emergency ex parte contacts.
key_cases.quote: We agree with Mother that her procedural due process rights were violated by the Appellees, though the individual defendants are protected by absolute immunity.

key_cases.case_name: Bayer v. Monroe County Children & Youth Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that even assuming a constitutional right to a post-removal hearing within seventy-two hours, that right was not clearly established such that the Pennsylvania caseworkers' conduct was objectively unreasonable.
key_cases.relevance: Addresses the timing of the post-custody hearing that must follow a Pennsylvania protective-custody seizure.
key_cases.quote: we consider it objectively reasonable for defendants to have believed, under the law existing at the time, that their particular conduct in this case was lawful

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the city and its caseworker, the court held that procedural due process does not require a parent's participation in an emergency ex parte custody hearing, and that a social worker's conduct in separating parent and child violates substantive due process only where it exceeds negligence and deliberate indifference and reaches gross negligence or arbitrariness that shocks the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why the protective-custody process may proceed ex parte without building in a pre-deprivation hearing whenever a parent happens to be available.
key_cases.quote: the standard of culpability for substantive due process purposes must exceed both negligence and deliberate indifference, and reach a level of gross negligence or arbitrariness that indeed "shocks the conscience."

key_cases.case_name: Mulholland v. Government County of Berks, Pennsylvania
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming judgment as a matter of law for the county, the court held that the CPSL's appeal process supplies all the process due to a person listed as an indicated perpetrator, so a county policy of not forwarding exculpatory information to ChildLine is not a constitutional violation, and that the removal rested on objectively reasonable suspicion.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that an unrebutted ChildLine listing can supply the reasonable suspicion needed to take children into care from the listed perpetrator's household.
key_cases.quote: That standard is met if the child is removed without "an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse," based on the information available at the time.

state_agency.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth, and Families

mandatory_reporters: Persons licensed or certified to practice in any health-related field under the jurisdiction of the Department of State (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(1))
Medical examiners, coroners and funeral directors (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(2))
Employees of a health care facility or provider licensed by the Department of Health who are engaged in the admission, examination, care or treatment of individuals (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(3))
Employees of a child-care service who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(5))

Clergymen, priests, rabbis, ministers, Christian Science practitioners, religious healers or spiritual leaders of any regularly established church or other religious organization (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(6))

Individuals, paid or unpaid, who on the basis of their role as an integral part of a regularly scheduled program, activity or service are responsible for the child's welfare or have direct contact with children (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(7))
Employees of a social services agency who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(8))
Peace officers and law enforcement officials (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(9))
Emergency medical services providers certified by the Department of Health (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(10))
Employees of a public library who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(11))
Individuals supervised or managed by a person listed under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(1) through (11) or (13) who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(12))

Attorneys affiliated with an agency, institution, organization or other entity, including a school or regularly established religious organization, that is responsible for the care, supervision, guidance or control of children (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(14))

Adult family members who are responsible for the child's welfare and provide services to a child in a family living home, community home for individuals with an intellectual disability or host home for children which are subject to supervision or licensure by the department under Articles IX and X of the Public Welfare Code (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(16))
reporting_details: Pennsylvania is not a universal-reporting state: only the categories of mandated reporters listed in 23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a) are required to report, and they must report immediately to ChildLine (1-800-932-0313) or electronically under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6313(a)(1) with a written report within 48 hours, while any other person may report to the department, the county agency or law enforcement under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6312.

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately if emergency protective custody is or may be required; otherwise see the child within 24 hours
timeline_requirements.starts_from: County agency receives the report from the Department of Human Services (ChildLine)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No consequence stated in 23 Pa.C.S. § 6368(b); county agency performance is reviewable by the department under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6343

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days in all cases; reasons for delay must be recorded if not completed within 30 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Investigation commenced by the county agency
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The particular reasons for delay past 30 days must be described in the child protective service record and made available to the department to determine whether the county agency strictly followed 23 Pa.C.S. Ch. 63 and whether it is subject to action under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6343
